structured_output.summary:
Ledger result: the four-body architecture, the tray/passage geometry, the spacer-frame openings and duct set, the full circulation path, lid-driven registration by rib and mating channel, gasket-after-registration sequencing, resilient-feet retention on shell ledges, the wick/condensate-channel option, the irreversible indicator option, and all three method claims trace cleanly to the USER disclosure (which is reproduced verbatim in the single USER turn of conversation.md). Claims 1-17 contain no limitation I could not trace, and the numeral table is one-to-one with the description. Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference, and "Not applicable" government-support statement match brief.md.

Nineteen problems remain. Eleven are untraced technical substance (reported critical). The largest cluster is the mechanical exposure indicator: FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 build an external housing standing proud of the shell wall and a horizontal bore through the wall thickness, plus a helical compression spring with named reaction surfaces, none of which the inventor disclosed beyond "visible from outside", "retained by a temperature-responsive latch" and "a spring moves the indicator stem". FIG. 3 verbalises internal flow boundaries the source never gives (cassette upper ends spaced below the upper web, communication with the ducts "across the upper parts of the cassettes", lower webs closing the frame underside beside the inlet), and adds joint substance to the rib/channel ("integral with" the lid, channel "to one side of the opening 46"). FIG. 1 insets the lid gasket from the perimeter; FIG. 5 and FIG. 2 place the condensate channel inside the base of the side supply passage between the shell wall foot and the tray wall and give it a depth/width proportion; FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 assign the tray perforations to specific surfaces and name what they open into. The detailed description adds three untraced operational assertions: the mis-set-module failure mode with outlets discharging against the tray or shell walls, "cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position", and "there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established".

Three internal inconsistencies are substantive. FIG. 1 makes the module "about the same outline in plan" as the tray, but FIG. 4 requires the frame to reach outboard over the side supply passages to the shell-wall ledges. FIG. 6 shows cassette 44 directly facing the inner surface of shell side wall 14 with nothing between, while FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 place the cassette's outboard surface, duct 48, the frame's outboard web, outlet 50 and side supply passage 30 between the cassette and that wall. FIG. 2 routes the descending passages straight down into the side supply passages, bypassing the peripheral outlet openings 50 that claim 1 and FIG. 4 make part of the path.

Two further disclosure gaps are graded major because the source is close but not affirmative: "the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction", and the between-journeys statements that the cassettes are "returned for conditioning" / "should be returned to conditioning intact" plus servicing "without dismantling the removable thermal module 40". Three minor items close the list: the density-difference mechanism attributed to the cassettes, parts numbered elsewhere left deliberately unnumbered in FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 (48, 24, 60), the closed-condition views resting the lid directly on the shell walls with no gasket 64 in the joint, and FIG. 4 discharging opening 56 into the side supply passage rather than into channel 70 as claim 6 recites.

No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain in any file, the line 2-2 designation is used consistently in FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and the Brief Description, and no application text justifies a renderer's shape choice with "by way of example" or "any closed outline" language. Every fix below is a deletion or a substitution of source-tracking wording and needs no new inventor input.

findings.title: Indicator housing standing proud of the shell wall and a bore through the wall thickness are untraced
findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md, bullets for 80 and 14; figures/FIG-2.md, bullet "Shell side wall 14"
findings.detail: The figure briefs build an external protruding housing with a closed outer end and a horizontal bore passing through the thickness of the insulated shell side wall. Both are substantive structure (a through-penetration of an insulated wall and an external enclosure). The disclosure says only that the shell includes an indicator that is visible from outside; it never describes a housing, a protrusion beyond the outer surface, an outer closure, or a bore. No affirmative source passage exists for any of these.
findings.evidence: Candidate, FIG-6.md: "Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a housing standing proud of the outer surface of the shell side wall 14, shown schematically as a hatched box of modest size, open toward the bore and closed at its outer end, its interior blank and aligned with the bore." and "A horizontal bore passes through its thickness, drawn as a blank passage between two hatched wall portions." Candidate, FIG-2.md: "A small housing, shown schematically, stands proud of the outer face of the left shell side wall 14, with a bore through that wall behind it." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch."
findings.fix: In FIG-6.md replace the indicator bullet with: "Mechanical exposure indicator 80: shown schematically as a plain rectangular outline at the outer part of the shell side wall 14, its interior blank and containing the stem 82, the latch 84 and the spring 86." Delete "A horizontal bore passes through its thickness, drawn as a blank passage between two hatched wall portions." and delete "open toward the bore", "closed at its outer end" and "aligned with the bore". In FIG-2.md replace the housing sentence with: "The mechanical exposure indicator is indicated schematically at the left shell side wall 14, shown as a plain outline without internal detail."

findings.title: Helical compression spring, its reaction surfaces and its compressed state are untraced
findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md, bullet for 86
findings.detail: The brief fixes the spring type (helical compression), its two anchoring surfaces (an internal surface of the housing and a face of the stem) and its loaded state. These are connection and operating-condition assertions, not a generic outline. The disclosure names only "a spring" that moves the stem outward.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Spring 86: a helical compression element in the interior of the housing, drawn as a series of connected loops between an inward-facing internal surface of the indicator 80 and a face of the stem 82, the loops closely spaced to show it under compression." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position." There is no source passage naming a spring type, an anchor surface, or a compressed state.
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: "Spring 86: shown schematically as a spring within the indicator 80 acting on the stem 82 in the outward direction." Delete "helical compression element", "between an inward-facing internal surface of the indicator 80 and a face of the stem 82", and "the loops closely spaced to show it under compression".

findings.title: FIG. 3 verbalises internal flow boundaries of the spacer frame that the disclosure never gives
findings.where: figures/FIG-3.md, bullets for 44 and 46 and the first summary bullet
findings.detail: The brief asserts (a) that each cassette's upper end is spaced below the upper web so that a transfer gap exists over the cassette tops, (b) that the inter-cassette space communicates with both ducts "across the upper parts of the cassettes", and (c) that the frame underside is closed on each side of the central inlet by lower web portions. All three are flow-boundary and flow-path statements, which remain substantive even in a schematic section. The disclosure states only that air "divides along faces of the cassettes" and "descends through the guide ducts"; it is silent on where the division occurs, on cassette height relative to the frame, and on whether the frame underside is closed beside the inlet.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "each having an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web and an upper end spaced below the upper web of the frame 42"; "The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 below it and with both ducts 48 across the upper parts of the cassettes 44, so that air entering the opening 46 passes along the opposed faces of the cassettes 44 and turns into the ducts 48."; "the lower web portions of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 on each side of it". Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages".
findings.fix: Delete "and an upper end spaced below the upper web of the frame 42" and "the lower web portions of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 on each side of it". Replace the summary bullet with: "The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 and with both ducts 48, so that air entering the opening 46 passes along the faces of the cassettes 44 and into the ducts 48."

findings.title: Rib-and-channel joint detail adds an untraced integral connection and an untraced channel location
findings.where: figures/FIG-3.md, bullets for 52 and 62
findings.detail: The rib and the mating channel form the registration joint, so statements about how the rib is attached and where the channel sits are substantive. The brief makes the rib integral with the lid underside and places the channel to one side of the central inlet opening with material on both sides. The disclosure says only that the lid "carries" a depending rib and that the frame has "a mating channel"; it never states integral formation or a lateral position relative to the inlet.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Depending indexing rib 62: a downwardly projecting hatched tongue integral with the underside of the lid 60"; "Mating channel 52: an upwardly open recess in the upper web of the frame 42, to one side of the opening 46 and bounded on both sides by hatched frame material." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame".
findings.fix: Replace with: "Depending indexing rib 62: a downwardly projecting hatched rib on the underside of the lid 60" and "Mating channel 52: an upwardly open recess in the upper web of the frame 42 that receives the rib 62." Delete "integral with", "to one side of the opening 46" and "bounded on both sides by hatched frame material".

findings.title: Lid gasket is placed inset from the lid perimeter, an untraced seal position
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md, bullet for 60
findings.detail: The gasket is a sealing member, so its position relative to the perimeter is substantive rather than a depiction convention. The disclosure states only that the gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration; it says nothing about the gasket being set in from the lid perimeter.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration."
findings.fix: Replace with: "A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band running all the way around it and facing the upper edge 16." Delete "set in from the perimeter".

findings.title: Condensate channel is located inside the base of the side supply passage and given a depth/width proportion
findings.where: figures/FIG-5.md, bullet for 70; figures/FIG-2.md, bullet "Shell floor 12"
findings.detail: The briefs form the channel as a trough in the upper surface of the shell floor lying between the foot of the shell side wall and the lower end of the tray side wall, that is, within the airflow supply passage, and add a depth-to-width proportion. Location within a flow path and proportions are substantive. The disclosure places the channel only "around the product tray" and calls it "shallow"; it does not say which body the channel is formed in, that it lies within the side supply passage, or how its depth compares with its width.
findings.evidence: Candidate, FIG-5.md: "Shallow condensate channel 70: an upwardly open trough in the upper surface of the shell floor 12, between the foot of the shell side wall 14 and the lower end of the tray side wall 24, its depth small compared with its width." Candidate, FIG-2.md: "its upper surface carrying a shallow upwardly open trough at each side beside the adjacent shell side wall 14". Nearest source (disclosure.md): "A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray."
findings.fix: In FIG-5.md replace with: "Shallow condensate channel 70: a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the removable product tray 20, shown schematically." Delete "in the upper surface of the shell floor 12, between the foot of the shell side wall 14 and the lower end of the tray side wall 24" and "its depth small compared with its width". In FIG-2.md replace the clause with "its upper surface carrying a shallow upwardly open trough around the tray 20, shown schematically".

findings.title: Tray perforations are assigned to particular tray surfaces and to particular passages
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md, bullet for 26; figures/FIG-2.md, bullet for 26
findings.detail: The briefs distribute the perforations between the upright tray walls and the bottom panel and state which passages each set opens into. That is flow-path topology, not a generic opening. The disclosure recites only "perforations in the product tray" as one step of the path and never allocates them to the tray walls, the tray floor, or to particular passages.
findings.evidence: Candidate, FIG-1.md: "Perforation 26: small through holes in the visible upright walls of the tray 20 and in its bottom panel, shown schematically." Candidate, FIG-2.md: "Perforation 26: small gaps through the upright panels and the bottom panel of the tray 20, opening into the adjacent side supply passage 30 and the lower return passage 28." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage".
findings.fix: In FIG-1.md replace with: "Perforation 26: small through holes in the removable product tray 20, shown schematically." In FIG-2.md replace with: "Perforation 26: small gaps through the panels of the tray 20, shown schematically." Delete "opening into the adjacent side supply passage 30 and the lower return passage 28"; the existing flow-arrow bullet already carries the disclosed path.

findings.title: Untraced mis-registration failure mode in the detailed description
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "The registered passive circulation path", paragraph beginning "The path exists only when"
findings.detail: The description asserts an exclusive condition for the path, a specific mis-set geometry in which the outlet openings discharge against the tray or shell side walls, blockage of the descending limb, and a resulting plain-insulated-box behaviour. None of this is disclosed. The inventor describes only the registered position; there is no affirmative passage describing an unregistered state, what the outlets face in that state, or how the carrier then performs. The Background discussion of displaced passages is prior-art context and cannot support invention text.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages."
findings.fix: Replace the two sentences with: "In the registered position the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30." Delete the remainder of the sentence beginning "If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position" up to "plain insulated box.", retaining the following sentence in the amended form: "This is what the registration described below establishes."

findings.title: Untraced assertion that the lid cannot close without carrying the module into position
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Lid-driven registration and retention", first paragraph
findings.detail: The description makes an absolute structural-functional assertion about the closing interlock: that the lid cannot reach the upper edge unless it has carried the module into position, and therefore that the packer cannot leave the module misaligned. The disclosure states that the rib shifts the module into the registered position as the lid closes; it never states that closing is obstructed or impossible when the module is out of position, and there is no affirmative passage about what the packer can or cannot leave behind.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position".
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "The person who packs the carrier is therefore not required to align the removable thermal module 40 separately, because closing the insulated lid 60 shifts it into the registered position."

findings.title: Untraced absolute statements that nothing is separately latched and that no unregistered closed state exists
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Lid-driven registration and retention", final paragraph
findings.detail: Two absolute negatives are asserted: that nothing must be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and that no closed-and-sealed state exists in which the path is not established. Neither is disclosed. The inventor describes the registration and the resilient-foot retention produced by closing, but gives no passage excluding other fasteners or checks, and no passage stating that a sealed-but-unregistered state is impossible.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport."
findings.fix: Delete the sentence, retaining the preceding sentence "Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event."

findings.title: FIG. 6 places the cassette directly against the shell side wall, contradicting FIG. 3 and FIG. 4
findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md, bullet for 44 and header; figures/FIG-3.md bullet for 48; figures/FIG-4.md bullets for 42, 50 and 30
findings.detail: FIG. 6 shows cassette 44 spaced just inboard of the inner surface of shell side wall 14 with nothing between them, so the stem's inner end at that surface faces the cassette. FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 place, in that same left-to-right section direction, the cassette's outboard surface, downward guide duct 48, the frame's outboard web, peripheral outlet opening 50 and side supply passage 30 between the cassette and the inner face of the shell side wall. The two depictions of the same section cannot both be right, and FIG. 6 is expressly tied to a region of the FIG. 2 section while also being described as being on an unspecified upright plane.
findings.evidence: FIG-6.md: "Phase-change cassette 44: a slab-like body inside the carrier at the right of the view ... spaced inboard of the inner surface of the shell side wall 14, the inner end of the stem 82 lying at that inner surface and thermally coupled to the facing surface of the cassette 44." versus FIG-4.md: "Rigid spacer frame 42: a hatched frame body below that slab, drawn as an upper horizontal web and an outboard upright web, the outboard web lying inboard of the shell side wall 14" and "Side supply passage 30: a blank open upright space below the peripheral outlet opening 50, between the inner face of the shell side wall 14 and an unnumbered hatched upright panel inboard of it"; and FIG-3.md: "Downward guide duct 48: two blank open upright passages, one on each side, each between the outboard surface of one cassette 44 and the nearer outboard web of the frame 42".
findings.fix: Make FIG. 6 a fragmentary view and remove the conflicting spacing. In the header add: "This is a fragmentary view; structures of the removable thermal module 40 other than the phase-change cassette 44 lie outside the plane of the view and are not shown." In the bullet for 44 replace "spaced inboard of the inner surface of the shell side wall 14, the inner end of the stem 82 lying at that inner surface and thermally coupled to the facing surface of the cassette 44" with "inboard of the shell side wall 14, the inner end of the stem 82 bearing against the facing surface of the cassette 44 so that the two are thermally coupled".

findings.title: FIG. 1 makes the module the same plan outline as the tray, which cannot reach the side supply passages or the shell ledges
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md, bullet for 40 and the bullet beginning "The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60"
findings.detail: The side supply passages lie between the tray side walls and the shell side walls, and the resilient feet bear on ledges of the shell side walls. A module that matches the tray in plan cannot overlie the side supply passages or reach the shell ledges, so FIG. 1 contradicts FIG. 4, the description and claims 1 and 3.
findings.evidence: FIG-1.md: "Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan". FIG-4.md: "Resilient foot 54: a downwardly projecting hatched foot at the outboard lower corner of the frame 42, in contact with and bearing down on the shelf of the ledge 18" and "the opening 50 overlaps the upper end of the side supply passage 30". draft/09-claims.md claim 1: "peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages".
findings.fix: Replace "about the same outline in plan" with "larger in plan than the tray 20 and about matching the opening of the shell 10 in plan, so that its periphery lies over the side supply passages".

findings.title: FIG. 2 routes the descending passages straight down into the side supply passages, bypassing the peripheral outlet openings
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md, bullets for 40 and "Flow arrows"
findings.detail: Claim 1 and the description make the peripheral outlet openings 50 part of the circulation path, and FIG. 4, the enlargement of the same region, shows duct 48 opening sideways through 50 into the top of side supply passage 30. FIG. 2, the view the Brief Description says shows the circulation path, instead has each descending passage open downward directly above a side supply passage and never depicts or numbers 50. The two views of the same junction disagree.
findings.evidence: FIG-2.md: "with two unnumbered descending passages either side of that opening, each opening downward above one side supply passage 30" and "down its two descending passages, down each side supply passage 30, through the perforations 26". FIG-4.md: "The duct 48 opens sideways through the peripheral outlet opening 50, and the opening 50 overlaps the upper end of the side supply passage 30 so that the two are in open communication." draft/09-claims.md claim 12: "through the peripheral outlet openings into the side supply passages".
findings.fix: In FIG-2.md replace the module bullet clause with: "with two descending passages 48 either side of that opening, each opening sideways at its lower end through a peripheral outlet opening 50 into the upper end of the adjacent side supply passage 30", amend the flow-arrow bullet to read "down its two descending passages 48, through the peripheral outlet openings 50, down each side supply passage 30", and add 48 and 50 to the numeral list for FIG. 2.

findings.title: Insulating construction attributed to "the walls that bound the interior"
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Overview of the carrier", first paragraph
findings.detail: The disclosure identifies only the outer shell and the lid as insulated. Extending insulating construction to "the walls that bound the interior" is a material assertion covering bodies the inventor never characterised, and the causal link drawn to reuse is likewise unstated.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be returned for reuse." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid."
findings.fix: Replace with: "The insulated outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are of insulating construction, and the carrier is reusable."

findings.title: Untraced reconditioning and module-dismantling statements in the servicing narrative
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Condensate handling and the removable wick" final paragraph and "Method of passively conditioning a payload" second paragraph
findings.detail: Three servicing assertions have no affirmative source. The disclosure states that conditioned cassettes are fitted before use, but never that cassettes are returned for conditioning between journeys, never that they "should be returned to conditioning intact", and never characterises wick replacement as avoiding dismantling of the module. The only disclosed servicing constraint is that the wick can be replaced without opening a cassette.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40"; "which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact"; "the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning". Nearest source (disclosure.md): "A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette." and "For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame".
findings.fix: Delete "and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40"; replace "which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact" with "which are conditioned before use"; and in the last paragraph delete "the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning," so the sentence reads "...withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position."

findings.title: Driving mechanism attributed to a density difference created by the cassettes
findings.where: draft/06-summary.md, paragraph beginning "The carrier is passive"; draft/08-detailed-description.md, "The registered passive circulation path", first paragraph
findings.detail: The disclosure states that the carrier is passive and that warm air rises from the product region. It does not state that circulation is produced by a density difference, nor that the cassettes create that difference. The mechanism statement is an added explanation of operation.
findings.evidence: Candidate (summary): "and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create." Candidate (description): "Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet ... The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."
findings.fix: In the summary delete ", and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create". In the description replace the sentence with: "Circulation is produced by warm air rising from the payload and air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that movement a single closed path to follow."

findings.title: Closed-condition views seat the lid directly on the shell walls with no gasket in the joint
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md, bullet for 60; figures/FIG-4.md, third bullet
findings.detail: Both closed-carrier views affirmatively show the lid resting on the shell side walls with nothing interposed, while the description and claim 2 require the compressible lid gasket 64 to be compressed against upper edge 16 once the carrier is closed. Omitting a part from a view is acceptable, but affirmatively seating the lid on the wall is inconsistent with the sealed condition.
findings.evidence: FIG-4.md: "An unnumbered horizontal hatched slab of substantial thickness spans the top of the view and rests on the upper end of the shell side wall 14." FIG-2.md: "Insulated lid 60: a horizontal hatched slab closing the top of the view, resting across both shell side walls 14 above the module 40." draft/08-detailed-description.md: "Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior."
findings.fix: In FIG-4.md replace with: "Insulated lid 60: a horizontal hatched slab of substantial thickness spanning the top of the view, with the compressible lid gasket 64 compressed between its underside and the upper edge 16 of the shell side wall 14", and add 16, 60 and 64 to the numeral list. In FIG-2.md amend the bullet to "...closing the top of the view above the module 40, the compressible lid gasket 64 being compressed against the upper edge of each shell side wall 14" and add 64 to the numeral list.

The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator does not control airflow.

For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame, products are placed in the tray, the thermal module is placed above the tray, and the lid is closed to register and retain the module. The disclosed essential relationship is the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration of the thermal module. The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features.

content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be returned and used again.
4	
5	The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
6	
7	Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.
10

Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.

Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be returned and used again.

The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

The removable thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The rigid spacer frame rests above the removable product tray and below the insulated lid. The rigid spacer frame includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages.

The circulation path therefore surrounds the payload rather than acting on it from one side, and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create.

content.content:
1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 at the centre of the rigid spacer frame 42 and facing the product region within the removable product tray 20, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration before the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
32	
33	Referring to FIG. 4, the same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.
34	
35	Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.
36	
37	## Condensate handling and the removable wick
38	
39	Referring to FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.
40	
41	The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.
42	
43	## Mechanical exposure indicator
44	
45	Referring to FIG. 6, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction, and the temperature-responsive latch 84 retains the indicator stem 82 against that action while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
46	
47	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
48	
49	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
50	
51	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
52	
53	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 after that registration. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
54	
55	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
56	
57	## Variations
58	
59	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be returned for reuse.

Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 at the centre of the rigid spacer frame 42 and facing the product region within the removable product tray 20, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration before the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

Referring to FIG. 4, the same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction, and the temperature-responsive latch 84 retains the indicator stem 82 against that action while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 after that registration. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

content.text: I've read all inputs, all ten draft sections, the numeral table, and all six figure briefs. Here is the complete review.

input.summary:
Preflight source-fidelity review of the p14 passive cold-chain carrier draft against input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (the two are textually identical; there is no second USER message, so the ledger authority is one paragraph block).

Filing formalities check out. The title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md ("No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."). No means-plus-function language appears. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain in any draft file. The abstract is 140 words, within the 150-word limit. The reference-numeral table is internally consistent: every numeral in numerals.md is used in the description, each numeral denotes exactly one part, and each figure brief's "Numerals shown on this figure" list matches the items actually verbalized in that brief. The section-line designation is consistent across all three places it must appear: FIG-1.md defines "line 2-2 ... the same section designation being repeated at each end of the line", FIG-2.md is "taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1", and draft/07-drawings.md recites "taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1". The four detail circles in FIG-2.md are unnumbered and are referred to by consistent positional wording in 07-drawings.md.

The independent-claim backbone traces cleanly. Every element of claim 1 and claim 12 other than the item in Finding 1 is affirmatively disclosed, including the shell/tray/module/lid architecture, tray feet and lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward to form two side supply passages, the rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes, the central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, the full circulation sequence, the "no fan, pump, or powered air mover" negative limitation, and lid-driven registration by the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel. Dependent claims 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 17 each trace to an exact sentence in the disclosure. Claims 5 and 15 (module lifts out as one piece with both cassettes; tray thereafter lifts out with the payload) follow directly from the disclosed removability and stacking order and are treated as supported. The optional-feature framing in the Summary and the Variations paragraph matches the disclosure's own statement that "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."

Thirteen findings follow. Six are critical disclosure_fidelity items, all of them verbalized geometric or flow relationships that the inventor never stated. Every one is in a functional flow boundary or contact interface, so the schematic-depiction allowance does not cover them: which passages the tray perforations open into; the side supply passages opening at their lower ends directly into the lower return passage (this one is also a claim 1 limitation, and it creates an undisclosed bypass around the disclosed perforation route); the crossover above the upper ends of the cassettes by which FIG-3 routes air from between the cassettes into the outboard ducts; the condensate channel verbalized as a trough formed in the upper surface of the shell floor between the shell wall foot and the tray wall; condensate discharge opening 56 verbalized as discharging into the side supply passage rather than into the channel, which also contradicts the disclosure's own "discharge condensate into the channel"; and the FIG-6 statement that the indicator stem ends at the wall's inner surface with the cassette spaced inboard of it, which asserts a specific non-contact coupling gap. In each case the underlying part is disclosed, so the fix strips the verbalized relationship and keeps a minimally specific generic depiction; no fix adds a speculative shape or a new optional embodiment to the application text.

Three findings are major internal_logic inconsistencies among the figure briefs. FIG-6 places a phase-change cassette directly facing the inner surface of the shell side wall, which cannot be reconciled with FIG-3 and FIG-4, where each cassette is separated from the shell wall by guide duct 48 and the frame's outboard web, or with FIG-2, where the module sits above the tray and the space beside the shell wall is the side supply passage. FIG-2, FIG-3 and FIG-4 all show the closed carrier with the lid resting directly on the shell side walls and omit compressible lid gasket 64, contradicting the description's statement that closing compresses the gasket against upper edge 16. FIG-2 routes the descending module passages downward directly into the side supply passages, bypassing the peripheral outlet openings 50 through which claim 12 and the description require the air to pass.

Four minor findings cover small unsupported characterizations in the description ("the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction"; "without dismantling the removable thermal module 40"; the "sealed" and "returned for conditioning" cassette characterizations) and two verbalized geometric choices in FIG-3 (cassettes "of equal size"; mating channel "to one side of the opening 46").

Background prior-art characterizations were not assessed for inventor support, per the standing instruction; they contain no citations for a later reviewer to trace. Per input/brief.md, no prior-art search was run and the art in prior_art/ may be incomplete.
